meaning: An origin, a set of axes and a unit (meters). A position only means something once you say which frame it is written in.
used: Every robot, car and drone; the Waymo Open Dataset defines global, vehicle, sensor and image frames

meaning: A frame fixed to the environment rather than the robot, such as a map or the take-off point. Landmarks keep the same coordinates in it.
A frame glued to the vehicle: in ROS x points forward, y left, z up. Body-frame coordinates change whenever the vehicle moves.
used: Obstacle avoidance, control; Waymo's vehicle frame

meaning: A frame attached to one sensor; every lidar, camera, radar and IMU reports its measurements in its own frame.
The ROS name for the robot's body frame, rigidly attached to the mobile base (REP 105).
A world-fixed frame in which the robot's pose is continuous (never jumps) but drifts without bound; published by odometry as odom → base_link.
used: Short-term local tasks such as obstacle avoidance

meaning: A world-fixed frame that should not drift but may jump when localization corrects itself; localization publishes map → odom.
The ROS standard for units (SI, radians) and axis conventions: x forward, y left, z up, ENU for geographic frames, z-forward optical frames for cameras, quaternions preferred.
The ROS standard naming the frames of a mobile robot (earth, map, odom, base_link), their guarantees, and who publishes each transform.
A local world frame with x east, y north, z up; the ROS convention for geographic frames.
used: ROS maps; Waymo Open Dataset global frame

meaning: A local world frame with x north, y east, z down, from aviation; positive altitude is negative z.
Two body-frame conventions: ROS uses FLU, PX4 and aviation use FRD; they differ by a 180° turn about the forward axis.
A camera frame with z out of the lens, x right and y down, matching image pixel directions; named with the _optical suffix in ROS.
A matrix whose columns are the rotated axes; multiplying a vector by it turns the vector, and its transpose undoes the turn.
A matrix with unit-length, mutually perpendicular columns, so RᵀR = I; rotations are the orthogonal matrices with determinant +1.
Rotating a point by θ (R) versus re-expressing a fixed point in a frame rotated by θ (Rᵀ); mixing them up is the classic sign bug.
Three angles describing an orientation as three turns about named axes in a fixed order; readable but singular somewhere and convention-dependent (24 variants).
Turns about the vertical, sideways and forward axes. In ZYX order, R = Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll). In ROS a positive pitch tips the nose down; in FRD it tips it up.
Turns about the moving body axes (intrinsic) versus about fixed axes (extrinsic); intrinsic ZYX equals extrinsic XYZ.
The loss of one degree of freedom in a three-angle representation when two rotation axes line up (pitch ±90° for ZYX); the angles stop being unique and their rates blow up.
used: Apollo's three-gimbal platform; reason drones store quaternions

meaning: Four numbers (w, x, y, z) = (cos θ/2, sin θ/2 · axis) storing a 3D rotation; unit length, no singularity, compose by the Hamilton product.
used: PX4 EKF2 attitude, PX4 attitude controller, all ROS messages

meaning: Quaternion multiplication; a ⊗ b means rotation a then b about the new body axes, and order matters.
q and −q represent the same rotation, so every orientation has two unit quaternions; compare them with |q₁ · q₂|.
Blends two quaternions along the shortest arc at a constant turn rate; the right way to interpolate orientations.
used: Animation, trajectory interpolation, pose interpolation in time

meaning: Dividing a quaternion by its length after numerical updates so it stays a pure rotation; far cheaper than re-orthonormalizing a matrix.
A matrix [[R, t], [0, 1]] (3×3 in 2D, 4×4 in 3D) that rotates and shifts a point written with an extra 1, so chaining frames is matrix multiplication.
Writing a point as (x, y, z, 1) and a direction as (x, y, z, 0), so translations act on points but not on directions; introduced by Möbius in 1827.
The pose of frame b in frame a, which maps b-coordinates to a-coordinates; chains cancel inner names: T_map_lidar = T_map_base · T_base_lidar.
The fixed transform from the vehicle body to a sensor (its extrinsics). Rotation errors in it grow with range: 1° is about 87 cm at 50 m.
used: Waymo per-sensor 4×4 extrinsics; Tesla camera self-calibration

meaning: The offset between a sensor and the vehicle's reference point; turning motion makes the sensor feel extra velocity and acceleration unless it's removed.
used: IMU and GNSS antenna offsets on drones and cars

meaning: Whether the data can pin down a parameter at all; repeated identical views (driving in a circle around a landmark) leave some calibration errors invisible.
The ROS 2 transform library: a time-buffered tree of frames that any node can publish to and query for any frame pair at any recent time.
The structure tf2 stores: each frame has exactly one parent, and lookups walk up to the common ancestor and back down, composing transforms.
Static links (sensor mounts) are published once on /tf_static with no history; dynamic links (odometry, joints) stream on /tf with timestamps.
The ROS message for one link: header (stamp, parent frame_id), child_frame_id, translation and quaternion rotation.
tf2's query: lookup_transform(target, source, time, timeout) returns the transform that maps source-frame data into the target frame at that time.
tf2's refusal to answer for a time outside its stored data: 'into the future' (newer than the latest message) or 'into the past' (older than the buffer).
tf2_ros command-line tool that publishes one fixed transform: --x --y --z, --yaw --pitch --roll (radians) or --qx..--qw, --frame-id, --child-frame-id.
An XML description of a robot's links and joints; robot_state_publisher turns it into static and joint transforms in tf2.
A chip with gyroscopes and accelerometers measuring turn rates and accelerations in its own frame; its mounting rotation must be known.
Open-source autopilot for drones and other vehicles; uses NED/FRD frames and represents attitude as a quaternion.
Tesla's name, at AI Day 2021, for the single vehicle-centered, top-down frame into which its networks fuse all eight cameras.
used: Tesla Autopilot / FSD perception (as publicly described)
